# Oath — A wallet, not a marketplace.

Oath is a self-custody Bitcoin and crypto wallet for iPhone and iPad. You control your wallet credentials, review fees before confirming, and manage supported assets without a trading marketplace.

- [Download Oath on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oath-bitcoin-crypto-wallet/id6780187283) — free, for iPhone and iPad
- [Features](https://oathwallet.org/features) · [Support](https://oathwallet.org/support) · [Press kit](https://oathwallet.org/press)

## Why Oath

Most crypto apps want you to trade. Oath wants you to own. No tickers shouting, no casino lights, no one holding your coins for you. Just your money, kept.

## What Oath supports

- Keep wallet credentials on your device and sign transactions locally.
- Create a recovery phrase, or use physical entropy with care.
- Restore supported wallet formats; keep any extra BIP-39 passphrase.
- Use optional password-encrypted iCloud backup with its matching backup file.
- Choose supported Bitcoin address types and inspect EVM approvals.
- Review network fees before confirming a transaction.
- Read the [public source and security scope](https://oathwallet.org/security).

Capabilities depend on the network and release. Silent Payments receiving and discovery are not supported in 4.1.14.

## App Store reviews

Rated **4.8 out of 5** from 38 ratings in the US App Store · checked October 30, 2026 on the App Store (reviews written when the app was named Aperture).

- “Impressed with the Security” — deebs.h: The interface is clean, easy to use, and it gives me confidence that privacy and security are taken seriously.
- “Love It” — Idwador iomp: Fast, secure, easy to use, and very reliable. Highly recommended!
- “Good to hold” — deweyrhodai: Good if you’re not into Web3 and just looking for a wallet to hold your funds.
- “Found it trending on X” — laneyodonnelly: A simple wallet… please keep it simple.

## Key facts

- **Formerly:** Aperture (Aperture Wallet). Oath was previously called Aperture (Aperture Wallet / “Aperture BTC Crypto Wallet” on the App Store). It is the same app, now renamed Oath Wallet; the source code repository is now named “oath-wallet”.
- **What it is:** Self-custody (non-custodial) crypto wallet
- **Platform:** iPhone and iPad (iOS / iPadOS), distributed on the Apple App Store
- **Price:** Free to download; users pay only blockchain network fees
- **Custody:** Oath never holds, controls or has access to user funds, private keys, recovery phrases or passkeys. It cannot recover, reverse or freeze transactions.
- **Accounts:** No account, email, phone number or KYC is required to use Oath.
- **Source code:** https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet
- **Contact:** care@oathwallet.org · X: https://x.com/OathWallet

<!-- oath-questions:start -->
## Self-custody, explained

### What is a self-custody crypto wallet?

A self-custody, or non-custodial, wallet lets you authorize transactions with your wallet’s private keys. The crypto remains recorded on its blockchain. Your wallet helps you manage the credentials and addresses used to access it. Keeping a usable recovery method is your responsibility.

[Understand Oath’s security model](https://oathwallet.org/security)

### How is a wallet different from an exchange account?

With a custodial exchange account, the provider controls the withdrawal keys. With self-custody, you manage the signing credentials. This removes reliance on an exchange to approve a withdrawal, but it also means a forgotten recovery phrase, a malicious approval or a mistaken transfer can cause permanent loss.

[Explore Oath Wallet features](https://oathwallet.org/features)

### Can I use Oath for Bitcoin and other crypto on iPhone?

Oath Wallet is available for iPhone and iPad. Choose the asset and network in the app before sharing a receiving address. A matching coin name or address format does not mean two networks are interchangeable. Available actions depend on your app version, network and wallet type.

[Check supported networks](https://oathwallet.org/networks)

### What happens if I lose my phone?

Recovery depends on the backup you prepared before the loss. A recovery phrase may also require its separate BIP-39 passphrase. Oath’s optional iCloud recovery needs the encrypted backup and the backup password. Check your recovery method before relying on it, and never share recovery words with support.

[Read the backup checklist](https://help.oathwallet.org/collections/backup)

### Is Oath free, and why do transfers have fees?

Oath is free to download from the App Store. Blockchain transfers can require network fees, account reserves or activation costs. These vary by network and conditions. Review the asset, destination, network and fee before confirming; an on-chain transfer generally cannot be reversed.

[Learn about network fees](https://articles.oathwallet.org/where-crypto-network-fees-actually-go)

### Does open source mean a wallet has been audited?

Public code lets people inspect an implementation. It does not by itself establish an independent security audit or prove that the app installed on a phone matches that code. Oath publishes its source-review scope and limitations so you can check the evidence behind a claim.

[Read about source and verifiable builds](https://articles.oathwallet.org/open-source-wallets-verifiable-builds)
<!-- oath-questions:end -->

# Oath features

Everything you need. Nothing you don’t.

## 01. Create or import a recovery phrase

New wallets use BIP39. Import supported BIP39, Electrum and aezeed phrases in their original format. Electrum and aezeed recover supported Bitcoin accounts and require manual recovery backups; they are not eligible for iCloud backup in 4.1.14.

## 02. Restore an encrypted backup

Restore an existing encrypted Oath backup using its backup password and the backup file in iCloud Drive. Keep a separate recovery-phrase backup and any extra BIP-39 passphrase.

## 03. 57 app localizations

Oath is available in 57 app localizations, with right-to-left layouts, local number formats and BIP39 word lists.

## 04. Open source, with a documented review scope

The full source code is public on GitHub at https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet. The published release includes its security model, verification record and reporting policy. Public source is available for review; it does not establish an independent audit or a verified match to the App Store binary.

## 05. Bitcoin address options

Compatible Bitcoin wallets support Taproot, Native SegWit, nested SegWit and Legacy, depending on the imported material. Capabilities vary by network. Oath 4.1.14 does not support Silent Payments receiving or discovery; see the Silent Payments guide before relying on that feature.

## 06. EVM Access

A tool that shows discovered token approvals (web3 permissions) on supported EVM networks and lets the user submit supported revocation transactions. Revoking is an on-chain transaction with a network fee shown before confirming.

## 07. Your display currency

Choose from the app’s supported display currencies. Values are estimates based on available exchange-rate data.

## 08. Available market prices

See available price quotes for supported assets. Quotes can be delayed or unavailable; displayed fiat values are estimates.

[Download Oath on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oath-bitcoin-crypto-wallet/id6780187283)

## Practical guides

Step-by-step help, with release notes and recovery limitations. Start with the guide that matches what you need to do.

# About Oath Wallet — Team, Open Source & Official Links

Oath Wallet is a free, open-source Bitcoin and crypto wallet for iPhone and iPad. The app was previously named Aperture Wallet.



## What Oath does

Oath is a self-custody wallet: you control the recovery credentials and authorize transactions on your device. It brings supported wallet imports, Bitcoin address choices, network-fee review, WalletConnect and optional encrypted iCloud backup into one app. Supported features depend on the network, wallet type and release.

[Explore the features](/features), [check the supported networks](/networks), or start with the [backup and recovery guide](/articles/backup-restore-oath-wallet).




## Publisher and team

The publisher identified in Oath’s legal and press information is STAGE AND STYLE COLLECTIVE LLC. Its published founder and CEO is Marco Valenti.

Follow the [official Oath Wallet account](https://x.com/OathWallet) and [Marco Valenti’s public profile](https://x.com/MarcoValentiX). The [press kit](/press#leadership) provides the company information and approved brand assets.




## Aperture became Oath Wallet

Oath Wallet is the new name of Aperture Wallet. The official App Store app retains the same app identifier, 6780187283. Existing references to Aperture in older reviews or screenshots describe that earlier name.

Use oathwallet.org for the website and the official App Store link below for the app. The app preserves its existing bundle, Keychain and iCloud container identifiers for compatibility.




## Open source and review scope

The [public source repository](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet) includes the code, license, review scope and security policy. The current source references were checked on October 30, 2026 against version 4.1.14 (98), commit v4.1.14. Version 4.1.14 (98) is a public source release. No App Store Connect upload or review submission was started for this source release. See the release record for completed checks.

Public source does not establish an independent security audit or prove that a particular App Store binary matches that source. [Read the security evidence and limitations](/security), including the release-specific Silent Payments restrictions.




## Product guides and corrections

Oath Editorial is the byline used for Oath’s product guides. These articles are product documentation, not independent security reviews. Updated guides identify the reviewed source release and label older screenshots. For corrections, use the support page; report sensitive vulnerabilities through the private GitHub channel.

## Help and vulnerability reports

For product guidance, use the [support page](/support) and [practical guides](/articles). For a security issue, follow the [repository’s reporting policy](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/policy). That policy describes the status of its private reporting channel; do not post exploit details in a public issue while arranging a private channel.

Never send a recovery phrase, private key, passphrase, backup credential or passkey to anyone claiming to be support. Oath cannot recover missing credentials or reverse an on-chain transaction.



[Download Oath Wallet](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oath-bitcoin-crypto-wallet/id6780187283)

# Oath Wallet Supported Networks

Choose the exact network before sharing an address. A matching ticker, logo or address prefix does not make networks interchangeable.

## Source and availability

This list follows all 36 networks in the [4.1.14 (98) import catalog](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Import/OathImportCatalog.swift), checked October 30, 2026. Build 98 is a source release with no Apple upload or review submission; installed versions can differ. Availability of tokens, imports and sending actions depends on the chain, wallet type and provider configuration.

## Bitcoin family

- Bitcoin
- Bitcoin Cash
- Litecoin
- Dogecoin

## Ethereum-compatible networks

- Arbitrum
- Arc
- Avalanche C-Chain
- Base
- BNB Smart Chain
- Ethereum
- Fantom
- Flare
- Gnosis
- Linea
- Optimism
- Polygon
- Celo
- Monad
- Unichain
- HyperEVM
- Robinhood Chain
- Scroll
- Somnia
- Story
- Taiko
- Telos
- X Layer

## Other account networks

- Aptos
- NEAR Protocol
- Solana
- Stellar
- Sui Network
- THORChain
- Gram
- TRON
- XRP Ledger

## Addresses, fees and recovery

Bitcoin address choices depend on the imported material. Compatible wallets can use Taproot, Native SegWit, nested SegWit and Legacy. Silent Payments receiving and discovery are not supported in 4.1.14. Electrum and aezeed imports recover supported Bitcoin accounts; aezeed does not restore Lightning channels or arbitrary custom LND accounts.

For an EVM token, check its chain and contract. The same 0x address format on several chains does not bridge assets between them. Arc uses USDC as its native fee asset; most other networks require their own native fee asset. Check the network and fee shown before signing.

Gram is the name used for the TON network in this source. Token identifiers, account reserves, activation costs, memos and destination tags differ by chain. A network appearing here does not mean every historical wallet format or token is supported.

## Before receiving

- Select the intended wallet, asset and network in Receive.
- Confirm that the sender offers that same network and asset deployment.
- Compare the complete destination; include a memo or tag when the receiving service requires it.
- Use your own app address, never an address from a help screenshot.
- Verify a restored account against a known original address before relying on it.

Read the [receiving guide](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/receive-crypto), [import guide](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/import-recovery-phrase), and [security model](https://oathwallet.org/security).

# Oath support

Contact a real person: **care@oathwallet.org** — put your iPhone model and app version in the message.

> **Oath will never ask for your recovery phrase, private key or passkey** — not by email, DM or call. Anyone who asks is trying to steal your wallet.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I create a wallet?

_Getting started_ — Open Oath and tap “Create a new wallet”. Your keys are generated on your iPhone, then you’ll back up your recovery phrase. Creating a local wallet needs no Oath account or email.

### Can I import a wallet from another app?

_Getting started_ — Yes. Choose Import wallet and use the original BIP39, Electrum or aezeed format with any required passphrase. Electrum and aezeed restore supported Bitcoin accounts. Private keys use a separate import with the matching network. Compare a known public address before moving funds.

### Can I create my own recovery phrase with dice?

_Getting started_ — The 4.1.14 source creates standard wallets with a 12-word BIP39 phrase. The earlier dice, coin-flip and typed-digit creation controls are not included in this release.

### What if I lose my iPhone?

_Backup & recovery_ — Install Oath on a compatible iPhone or iPad and use the correct recovery phrase and any extra passphrase, or an existing encrypted iCloud backup with its backup password. Your funds live on the blockchain, not on your phone.

### Can Oath recover my recovery phrase?

_Backup & recovery_ — No. Recovery material is protected locally in the app, not held by Oath support. Keep your own recovery backup; support cannot replace missing words, keys or passwords.

### How does encrypted backup restore work?

_Encrypted backups_ — An existing Oath iCloud backup needs both the encrypted backup file in iCloud Drive and its backup password. Keep iCloud Drive and the backup password available on the new device, then follow Restore from iCloud. Apple Account access alone is not enough.

### Is an iCloud backup a replacement for my recovery phrase?

_Encrypted backups_ — For eligible wallets, it is an additional recovery method. Keep manual recovery material too. Electrum and aezeed wallets are excluded from iCloud backup in 4.1.14.

### Why is my transaction pending?

_Sending & receiving_ — Transactions confirm when the network includes them. Busy networks take longer. You can see the status and the fee you paid in the transaction details.

### What are network fees?

_Sending & receiving_ — Fees go to the network, not to Oath. A network-fee estimate is shown before you confirm; the final fee can depend on the network and transaction.

### Which address type should I use for Bitcoin?

_Sending & receiving_ — Native SegWit (bc1q) and Taproot (bc1p) are efficient Bitcoin address options. The best choice depends on sender compatibility and how your coins will be spent. Nested SegWit and Legacy are also available where supported by the imported material. Silent Payments receiving and discovery are not supported in 4.1.14.

### Someone from “Oath support” asked for my phrase.

_Security_ — That is a scam. Oath will never ask for your recovery phrase, private key or passkey. Don’t reply, and forward the message to care@oathwallet.org.

### Is Oath open source?

_Security_ — Yes. The full source is published on GitHub at github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet, with a current security model, release verification record and security policy. Public source does not establish an independent audit or a verified match to the App Store binary.

### What is EVM Access?

_EVM Access_ — A tool that shows discovered token approvals on supported EVM networks. Revoke a supported permission with an on-chain transaction; a network fee applies.

### Does revoking an approval cost a fee?

_EVM Access_ — Yes, a small network fee, because revoking is an on-chain transaction. Oath shows it before you confirm.

## Practical guides

Step-by-step help, with release notes and recovery limitations. Start with the guide that matches what you need to do.

- [Choose a backup and restore method](/articles/backup-restore-oath-wallet)
- [Move Oath to a new iPhone](/articles/move-oath-to-new-iphone-direct-encrypted-serverless)
- [Import an existing or older wallet](/articles/recovery-phrase-private-key-icloud-iphone-transfer-import)
- [Understand Bitcoin address types](/articles/bitcoin-settings-oath-address-types-indexes-complete-guide)
- [Receive on the correct network](/articles/receive-crypto-safely-network-address-qr-requested-amounts)
- [Check Silent Payments availability and limits](/articles/silent-payments-oath-reusable-bitcoin-address-without-reuse)

[Check supported networks](/networks) · [Read the security evidence](/security)

## Security vulnerabilities

Use [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/advisories/new) and follow the [security policy](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/policy). Reports go privately to repository maintainers. Never include real wallet credentials or post exploit details in a public issue.

## About Oath (boilerplate)

Oath is a self-custody Bitcoin and crypto wallet for iPhone and iPad, built on one idea: a wallet, not a marketplace. Keys are created and kept on the user’s device — Oath never holds them. People can create a new BIP39 wallet or import supported BIP39, Electrum and aezeed recovery material, restore an existing encrypted iCloud backup with its backup password, and use Taproot, SegWit, Legacy where supported by the imported material. The app is open source, with a documented security scope.

# Oath Wallet security

Oath Wallet keeps recovery input and signing credentials in its protected local vault. Optional encrypted iCloud backups, deliberate exports and WalletConnect requests have separate user-controlled boundaries.

## Open source and App Store builds

The technical descriptions and source excerpts on this page were checked on 30 October 2026 against Oath Wallet **4.1.14 (98)**, source tag **v4.1.14**. Version 4.1.14 (98) is a public source release. No App Store Connect upload or review submission was started for this source release. See its release record for the completed checks; source publication does not establish a match to an App Store download.

Read the [4.1.14 release verification record](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/releases/tag/v4.1.14), [current security model](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/main/Documentation/SecurityModel.md), and [security reporting policy](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/policy). Provider configuration and Apple signing are supplied through encrypted GitHub deployment secrets and excluded from public source.

## What the checks establish

The release record covers source inspection, secret scanning, compilation and focused host tests. No simulator or physical-device checks were run for build 98. It does not establish an independent security audit or an independently reproduced comparison with an App Store download. Apple approval alone would not establish either result.

## Recovery formats and local signing

New standard wallets use a 12-word BIP39 recovery phrase. BIP39 imports validate supported word lists and checksums locally. Electrum and aezeed imports use their own formats and restore supported Bitcoin accounts; they are not reinterpreted as BIP39. Preserve any required original passphrase and compare known public addresses after import.

Private-key imports retain their network scope. Multisignature wallets retain their signer material and policy locally; support and required setup differ by chain. Keeping several signing keys on one device does not provide independent-device security. A wallet name or successful import does not establish that every previous account has been recovered.

Source: [mnemonic validation](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Import/OathMnemonicValidator.swift), [wallet engine](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathWalletEngine.swift), [private-key import](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathPrivateKeyImport.swift), and [multisignature creation](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathMultisigCreation.swift).

## Local storage and app lock

Wallet secrets are sealed in an authenticated AES-GCM vault, stored through non-synchronizing, device-only Keychain storage. An additional installation key is kept in a protected, backup-excluded app-container file. When enabled, the app passcode protects the vault key using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds. Biometrics and the selected auto-lock delay control access. Disabling the app passcode changes that protection; device compromise remains a risk.

Public wallet records, balances and history are stored separately in the local database. Removing the app also removes its installation key; do not treat reinstalling as a recovery method.

Source: [vault envelope](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathVaultEnvelope.swift), [vault storage](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathInstallationVaultStorage.swift), [installation protection](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathInstallationSecurity.swift), and [lock policy](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Security/OathSecurityPolicy.swift).

## Password-encrypted iCloud backup

For supported wallets, Oath creates a .oathbackup file encrypted on the device with AES-256-GCM. A separate backup password derives its key using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds and a fresh 32-byte salt. Restore needs both that encrypted file and its password. The app passcode, a passkey, or Apple Account access alone cannot decrypt it.

Each eligible wallet has its own file. Electrum and aezeed wallets are excluded from iCloud backup in 4.1.14; preserve their original recovery words and required passphrase. Back Up All Wallets covers eligible active wallets, not Recently Deleted wallets. Verify each upload result. Existing iCloud files remain outside the local app-reset boundary.

Source: [backup format](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/Packages/OathCloudBackup/Sources/OathCloudBackup/BackupDocument.swift), [backup eligibility](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathWalletVault.swift), and [restore flow](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathCloudRestoreModel.swift). See the [backup guide](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/backup-password).

## Network and diagnostic boundaries

This source release has no operator endpoint for wallet credentials, recovery typing, wallet records or diagnostic uploads. Privacy-filtered diagnostics remain in a bounded local outbox. Blockchain providers still receive public queries for balances, fees and history, and signed transactions for broadcast. WalletConnect uses encrypted relay connections for user-approved sessions and signing requests. A signature, accepted broadcast and confirmed transaction are different outcomes.

Source: [local EVM signing](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathEVMSigning.swift), [send service](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Send/OathEVMSendService.swift), and [WalletConnect details](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/Documentation/WalletConnectReadableDetails.md).

## Recovery limits

The 4.1.14 source does not provide Silent Payments receiving or discovery, the former nearby-iPhone transfer flow, or dice/coin/digit wallet creation. Its Bitcoin receive options depend on the imported material. Aezeed recovery covers supported on-chain Bitcoin branches, not Lightning channels or arbitrary custom LND accounts. Do not erase an older wallet until a supported recovery method reproduces its intended accounts. Never fund a public tutorial phrase or an example address.

Source: [import catalog](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/OathAtmosphere/Import/OathImportCatalog.swift), [Bitcoin keys](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/v4.1.14/Packages/OathBitcoin/Sources/OathBitcoin/BitcoinKeys.swift), and [aezeed scope](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/main/Packages/OathAezeed/README.md).

## Report a vulnerability

Use [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/advisories/new). Include the affected version and reproduction steps using unfunded test material. Never send a real recovery phrase, private key, passphrase or backup password. Oath support cannot replace a missing recovery credential.

## 3. What the Service is

Oath is a non-custodial (self-custody) wallet: software that runs on your device and helps you generate keys, view balances and sign transactions on public blockchains.

Oath is not a bank, exchange, broker, payment institution, custodian, investment adviser or marketplace. We never hold, control or have access to your digital assets, private keys, recovery phrase or passkeys, and we cannot execute transactions for you.

## 4. Your keys, your responsibility

Recovery requires the credentials appropriate to your wallet: its recovery words and any required passphrase, private keys, or a supported encrypted backup and its password. You are solely responsible for creating, storing and protecting them.

- Keep original recovery credentials private and verify the supported import format before relying on recovery.

## 5. Transactions and fees

Transactions are broadcast to public networks that we do not control, and are irreversible once confirmed. Network fees are paid to network participants, not to Oath, and are shown before you confirm.

# Privacy Policy

Last updated: October 30, 2026

**In short:** No account signup, email or KYC is required to use the wallet. You control the wallet credentials. The App Store version of Oath Wallet does not send us app analytics or automatic error reports. Optional encrypted backups, deliberate exports, WalletConnect and network services and the website's separate features have the data boundaries described below. We do not sell personal data or share it for cross-context behavioural advertising.

## 1. Who we are

This Privacy Policy explains how STAGE AND STYLE COLLECTIVE LLC, 2103 Condor Ct, Redmond, Oregon 97756-8281, United States (“Oath”, “we”, “us”) handles personal data when you use Oath Wallet distributed through the App Store and the Oath website (the “Service”). We are the data controller for the limited personal data described here.

Contact: care@oathwallet.org.

## 2. Our approach

The App Store app does not collect user analytics or automatically upload error reports. Network requests, optional services, website visits and information you choose to send us are described separately below. We do not require an account, name, email address, phone number or identity documents to use the wallet app or browse the website. The optional newsletter requires an email address.

## 3. Wallet credentials and device storage

In the 4.1.14 public source, recovery material is sealed in an authenticated local vault using device-only Keychain storage and an additional installation key in the protected app container. Public wallet metadata and transaction records are stored separately in the local database. Signing takes place locally; network providers receive public queries and signed transactions, not the spending credentials used to sign them.

Optional encrypted iCloud backup can store eligible wallet material at your request. Manual export can also reveal or copy recovery material under your control. Do not interpret on-device storage as a promise that a user-authorized export never leaves the device.

Face ID and Touch ID are handled by iOS; Oath does not receive your biometric templates. Public source publication does not independently establish a match to a distributed App Store binary. See [the security evidence and version scope](https://oathwallet.org/security).

## 4. Password-encrypted backup and WalletConnect

Optional iCloud backup encrypts an eligible wallet on the device with AES-256-GCM. Its key is derived from a separate backup password using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds and a fresh salt. Restore requires both the encrypted backup file and its backup password. Oath does not receive the password or a plaintext backup. Apple operates iCloud Drive under its own policies.

Electrum and aezeed wallets are not eligible for iCloud backup in 4.1.14; preserve their original recovery material. Existing backup files remain outside the app-reset boundary. The former passkey-based backup and nearby-iPhone transfer flows are not current recovery methods. Keep an older device until a supported recovery method is verified.

WalletConnect uses encrypted relay connections to pair with a dApp. A user-approved connection can share public accounts and requested signatures or signed transactions with that dApp. It does not send recovery phrases or private keys. Review the destination and request before approving.

## 5. Data processed to provide the Service

To show balances, prices and history and to broadcast transactions, the app connects to blockchain nodes and price-data services. These requests can reveal:

- Your public wallet addresses and transactions (which are public on blockchains by design)
- Your device’s IP address and basic technical information (such as app version and device type)
- Your chosen display currency and language

## Notification services in earlier releases

The 4.1.14 public source does not register wallet addresses or notification tokens with an operator notification service. Earlier releases and separately enabled services may have registered public wallet information, notification tokens and device metadata. Contact us about data you previously supplied to those services; updating the app alone does not delete earlier service records.

## Website visitor statistics

On oathwallet.org, we use first-party website analytics to understand visits and App Store download-button clicks. A random, first-party browser identifier is stored in a Secure, HttpOnly cookie for up to one year. Session information in your browser groups activity into visits after 30 minutes of inactivity. We record page paths (not query strings), referral domains (not full referral URLs), broad browser/device categories, and approximate country/city and rounded coordinates derived by Cloudflare from your IP address. This is not GPS location and does not request device-location access. Our analytics records do not store your raw IP address or link visits to wallet data.

Restricted administrators can view statistics, anonymous returning-browser history, and visit/download alerts in the restricted administration console. Detailed events are retained for up to 400 days. Clearing the cookie creates a new anonymous browser identity. We exclude detected automated traffic and honour Global Privacy Control and Do Not Track signals. You can enable those browser settings to opt out of this website analytics. Download clicks are not evidence of app installation.


## Optional Oath Notes newsletter

If you choose to subscribe, we store your email address, selected topics, signup source page, consent version and timestamps, subscription status and signup method, and subscription changes to provide the newsletter. Newsletter signup is optional and is not connected to wallet addresses, balances, recovery phrases, or private keys. Submitting the signup form subscribes you immediately; no email confirmation is required. Emails may include Oath Wallet releases, crypto news and market prices, security alerts, and practical guides.

Our email delivery provider processes the recipient address and message content. We record sending, delivery, bounce, complaint, and unsubscribe events. When engagement measurement is enabled for a campaign, tracking pixels and redirect links can report opens and clicks. These are approximate signals: email privacy services and security scanners may create events without a person reading or clicking. We do not store the IP addresses or user-agent strings received in newsletter event reports.

You can change topics or unsubscribe using the private link in an email. Unsubscribed addresses and permanent delivery failures are suppressed from future campaigns. We retain subscription and consent records while needed to deliver the newsletter, honour opt-outs, and resolve delivery or abuse issues. Contact care@oathwallet.org to request access or deletion; a minimal suppression record may be retained to prevent future unwanted messages.

The website remembers that the signup dialog appeared using browser local storage and a preference cookie (up to 400 days). This preference does not identify you and is not linked to subscriber records. It stops repeated prompts in that browser. Clearing browser storage, private browsing, or using another device can show the dialog again. Short-lived, keyed IP hashes help limit automated signup and login attempts; raw IP addresses are not saved in the newsletter database.

## 6. App analytics and error reports

The App Store version of Oath Wallet does not automatically upload app errors, crash reports, usage analytics or diagnostic logs to our servers. Website visitor statistics and information you voluntarily send to support are separate from the app and are described in this policy.

If you choose to share analytics with app developers in iOS settings, Apple may provide us with aggregated crash reports and performance data that do not identify you. You can change this at any time in Settings › Privacy & Security › Analytics & Improvements.

## 7. Support requests

If you contact care@oathwallet.org, we process your email address and the contents of your message to respond. Never include your recovery phrase or private keys.

## 8. Why we process data (legal bases)

Where laws such as the EU/UK GDPR apply, we rely on:

- Performance of a contract — to provide the Service you request (connecting to networks, showing prices)
- Legitimate interests — to keep the Service secure, prevent abuse and fix bugs, balanced against your rights
- Consent — for the optional newsletter, which you can withdraw at any time
- Legal obligation — where we must comply with applicable law

## 9. What we don’t do

We do not sell personal data, “share” it for cross-context behavioural advertising, build advertising profiles, use third-party ad trackers, or make decisions about you based solely on automated processing that produce legal effects.

## 10. Sharing with service providers

We may use a small number of service providers (such as blockchain node providers, price-data providers, hosting and email providers) who process data on our behalf under written contracts that require confidentiality and security. We may disclose information where required by law or to protect rights and safety, and we will resist over-broad requests where the law allows.

## 11. International transfers

Our providers may process data in countries other than yours. Where required, we protect transfers with appropriate safeguards such as the European Commission’s Standard Contractual Clauses, the UK International Data Transfer Addendum, or other lawful transfer mechanisms.

## 12. Retention

Network and price requests are not stored by us beyond what our providers need for security logs (typically no longer than 30 days). Support emails are kept only as long as needed to resolve your request, then deleted, unless we must keep them by law.

## 13. Security

The published source uses device-only Keychain storage, local signing, authenticated encryption for the local vault and optional iCloud backup, and encrypted network connections. Blockchain private keys are not described as Secure Enclave signing keys. The version-specific evidence and limitations are documented at https://oathwallet.org/security; published source is available at https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet.

## 14. Your rights

Depending on where you live, you may have the right to access, correct, delete or port your personal data, to object to or restrict processing, and to withdraw consent. Removing the app removes its installation key, but does not delete separate iCloud backups or earlier service records; use the deletion methods described below. To exercise any right, email care@oathwallet.org. We will respond within the time required by law and will not discriminate against you for exercising your rights.

You also have the right to complain to your local data-protection authority.

## 15. Regional information

We aim to meet the requirements of privacy laws worldwide, including:

- European Union, EEA and United Kingdom — GDPR and UK GDPR
- United States — CCPA/CPRA (California) and other state privacy laws; we honour Global Privacy Control signals, and we do not sell or share personal information
- Brazil — LGPD
- Canada — PIPEDA and applicable provincial laws
- Australia — Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles
- Japan — APPI · South Korea — PIPA · Singapore — PDPA · Thailand — PDPA
- India — Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
- China — PIPL
- Saudi Arabia — PDPL · United Arab Emirates — PDPL · Türkiye — KVKK
- South Africa — POPIA · Nigeria — NDPA · Kenya — Data Protection Act

## 16. Children

The Service is not directed to children under 13 (or under 16 where required by local law), and we do not knowingly collect their personal data. If you believe a child has contacted us, email care@oathwallet.org and we will delete the information.

## 17. Deleting your data

Use the app’s wallet-removal or reset controls for their supported local deletion scope, and verify your independent recovery material first. Deleting the app alone does not guarantee removal of Keychain items. iCloud backups are outside the app-reset boundary and must be managed separately through your iCloud storage. Assets remain on their blockchains; future access depends on retaining the correct recovery material and any required passphrase or output-specific information. To delete support correspondence, email care@oathwallet.org from the address you used.

## 18. Changes to this policy

We will post any changes here and update the “Last updated” date. For material changes, we will notify you in the app before they take effect.

Questions: care@oathwallet.org
